title: Money Before the Mint
summary: What would you accept as payment? Six coins and notes show how money worked in early America, including a forgery made to pass for the real thing.
introduction: Before the U.S. Mint was established in 1792, people in America paid with coins from overseas and paper issued closer to home. Look at three pairs: two Spanish silver coins, an authorized note beside a counterfeit, and two copper portraits on opposite sides of independence. Each offers a different reason to accept a payment, and a reason to look twice.

curatorialLens.label: What made it money?
curatorialLens.description: Six objects, three close comparisons. Look for the metal, the wording, and the name of the authority behind a payment.

experience.overview: Start with the silver, compare the two notes, then turn over the coppers. Each display holds just two objects; open either one to see its details.

groups.title: A dollar from Spain
groups.description: The Spanish dollar was familiar money in British North America. Beside it is a smaller Spanish real. Look for the castles, lions, and royal arms: these coins announced one monarchy, but silver could find takers beyond its borders.

groups.title: The promise and the forgery
groups.description: The North Carolina note cites an act of its Assembly. The New Jersey note claims that it shall pass by law, but this example is a contemporary counterfeit. Compare the official language and handwritten marks that make both pieces of paper look like money.

groups.title: A new authority, a familiar face
groups.description: Virginia puts George III on its halfpenny. Fourteen years later, Connecticut still uses a portrait bust, but names the state as its authority. Compare the lettering around the heads, then turn the coins over. Independence changed the message without abandoning familiar designs.

tourStops.title: A dollar from Spain
tourStops.narration: The dollar in this case is Spanish. Coins of this denomination, also called pieces of eight, were widely used in British North America. Compare it with the smaller real: both carry Spanish symbols. The country named on a coin did not set the limits of where its silver could be accepted.

tourStops.title: Even a forgery could invoke the law
tourStops.narration: Open the New Jersey note and find the words "by LAW shall pass current." This is a contemporary counterfeit. Its maker copied the language of legal authority along with the appearance of money. Beside it, the North Carolina bill names an act of the Assembly. What on either note would have reassured the person taking it?

tourStops.title: Look past the portrait
tourStops.narration: These heads look at home beside each other. Virginia shows George III; Connecticut keeps the bust format but names a different authority. On the Connecticut coin, look for AUCTORI CONNEC, meaning "by the authority of Connecticut." Turn it over for the seated figure and the abbreviated declaration of independence and liberty.

tourStops.title: Money had to pass from hand to hand
tourStops.narration: The silver offered recognizable metal. The notes claimed legal backing, even when that claim was forged. The coppers put authority into a familiar design. All still needed someone willing to take them. Return to any pair and look again at the detail you would have trusted.

artifacts.title: Spanish Eight Reales, 1701–1759
artifacts.description: This is the denomination behind the phrase "piece of eight": eight reales, also known as a Spanish dollar. Coins like it were widely accepted in British North America. Their silver gave them a use far beyond the territories ruled by Spain. This example is cataloged broadly to 1701-1759; its exact date and mint remain unconfirmed.
artifacts.subtitle: The Spanish dollar
artifacts.origin: Spanish monetary world; mint attribution pending
researchNotes: The collection record currently supplies a broad 1701–1759 attribution.
A future attribution pass should establish the ruler, mint, date, weight, and variety before the label becomes more specific.

artifacts.title: 1759 Spanish One Real
artifacts.description: Look for the castles and lions on one side, then the crowned shield on the other. This smaller silver coin is cataloged as a one real struck at Seville in 1759. Beside the eight-reales piece, it shows another denomination in Spanish silver. The designs identify royal authority; they do not tell us where this particular coin traveled.

images.alt: Silver Spanish real showing a quartered design of castles and lions inside a shaped border
images.caption: The quartered castles and lions identify Castile and León.

images.alt: Silver Spanish real showing a crowned royal shield surrounded by a worn inscription
images.caption: The crowned arms place royal authority at the center of the coin.

artifacts.subtitle: Spanish symbols on a smaller coin
researchNotes: The source catalog identifies this object as a 1759 Seville one real.
A type comparison for Ferdinand VI's one-real coinage identifies the crowned royal arms, Castile-and-León design, silver composition, and Seville mint mark.
Further object-level attribution, weight, and die study should be completed before presenting a more specific variety.

artifacts.title: 1754 North Carolina Forty Shillings
artifacts.description: The large words "Forty Shillings" name the value. Beneath them, the bill cites an act of North Carolina's Assembly dated March 9, 1754. A church appears at the lower left; handwritten marks complete the printed form. The paper carries a claim backed by colonial authority. Compare that claim with the one copied on the New Jersey counterfeit.

images.alt: North Carolina forty-shilling bill with Assembly authorization, handwritten marks, and a church vignette
images.caption: Below the denomination, the bill cites an act of the Assembly dated March 9, 1754.

artifacts.subtitle: Forty shillings by act of the Assembly
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the denomination and date as forty shillings, 1754.

artifacts.title: 1763 New Jersey Twelve-Shilling Counterfeit
artifacts.description: "By LAW shall pass current": the wording sounds emphatic, but this twelve-shilling bill is cataloged as a contemporary counterfeit. Notice its ornamental border, handwritten number, and sweeping signatures. Those details imitate the appearance of an authorized issue. The North Carolina note beside it is a different colony's money, not a matching original for authenticating this forgery.

images.alt: Counterfeit New Jersey twelve-shilling bill with an ornamental border, handwritten number, and signatures
images.caption: The counterfeit repeats the claim "by LAW shall pass current."

images.alt: 1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit, photograph 2

artifacts.subtitle: A forgery that claims the force of law
researchNotes: The collection record identifies this object as a contemporary counterfeit of the December 31, 1763 twelve-shilling issue.

artifacts.title: 1773 Virginia Halfpenny
artifacts.description: George III faces right on this halfpenny. Turn it over to find a crowned shield and Virginia's name. Struck in London for the colony, the issue is dated 1773 but was released in 1775. Compare its portrait with the Connecticut copper: the later coin keeps a familiar format while changing the authority named around it.

images.alt: Copper Virginia halfpenny showing a worn right-facing portrait of King George the Third
images.caption: George III occupies the portrait side beneath a Latin royal inscription.

images.alt: Copper Virginia halfpenny showing a crowned shield divided into heraldic sections
images.caption: Virginia's name surrounds a crowned shield on the reverse.

artifacts.subtitle: The king on Virginia's small change
artifacts.origin: Tower Mint, London; issued for Virginia
researchNotes: Colonial Williamsburg identifies the issue as the only colony-specific coinage fully authorized by the Crown and notes archaeological evidence of use in Williamsburg.
The National Museum of American History records the right-facing portrait of George III and crowned Virginia shield on the 1773 halfpenny.
The exact die variety of this collection example has not yet been assigned.

artifacts.title: 1787 Connecticut Copper
artifacts.description: The bust may look royal, but the inscription names Connecticut. AUCTORI CONNEC means "by the authority of Connecticut." On the reverse, a seated figure accompanies INDE ET LIB, an abbreviation for independence and liberty. This 1787 copper uses the visual language of British small change to carry the authority of a state.

images.alt: Worn copper Connecticut coin showing a right-facing bust and portions of the AUCTORI CONNEC inscription
images.caption: The portrait side transfers authority from a monarch to Connecticut.

images.alt: Worn copper Connecticut coin showing a seated classical figure with staff
images.caption: A seated figure evokes liberty through a visual form familiar from British copper.

artifacts.subtitle: A portrait without a king's name
researchNotes: The American Numismatic Society places Connecticut among the states that authorized copper coinage under the Articles of Confederation.
The design's classical seated figure and abbreviated Latin legends show how new political claims could inhabit older-looking forms.
A future catalog pass should assign the exact Miller die variety.
